prompt: What happened to Coreto's cloud bill each month before Davi started on it?
hint: Who opens it, and who makes the decisions on it?

choices.text: Platform reviewed it line by line
choices.why: Rafaela's team read it for the first time with Davi; that was the change.

choices.text: Each team lead received their own part of it
choices.why: That is the showback Davi built afterwards, not the starting point.

choices.text: Finance paid it unread by engineering
choices.why: Right: the people who see the bill cannot change it, and the people who change it do not see it.

choices.text: The CTO approved it after a monthly review
choices.why: A monthly review is the operate phase Coreto set up later.

prompt: Put the FinOps Foundation's three phases in the order the lesson takes them.
hint: You cannot save on what nobody can see.
trap: Optimising first produces savings nobody understands, which is why they decay.

prompt: A consultant's cost-cutting project lowers the bill for a quarter, and then it climbs back. What reason does the lesson give?
hint: Who made the savings, and who makes the decisions?

choices.text: The provider raised its prices
choices.why: Prices change, but the lesson's reason is about who decides, not about the price list.

choices.text: The tool bought for it was the wrong one
choices.why: A better tool would meet the same problem: the people deciding never saw the bill.

choices.text: Traffic grew faster than the savings
choices.why: Growth would show in the unit cost; the lesson blames the way the savings were made.

choices.text: It was made by people who do not decide
choices.why: Right: the decisions carried on as before, so the waste came back with them.

prompt: Coreto's provider replaces the discount scheme Coreto had committed to with a new one. Which part of this lesson needs revisiting?
hint: What ages, and what does not.

choices.text: The unit cost, since the bill is now priced differently
choices.why: Unit cost asks about the business, so it survives the change: the ticket count and the bill still divide.

choices.text: The terms of the commitment, while the questions stand
choices.why: Right: the mechanism is the part that ages. What a ticket costs, who spent it and whether anybody uses it do not.

choices.text: The showback, because tags belong to the old scheme
choices.why: Tags name owners and have nothing to do with a discount scheme.

choices.text: The whole lesson, as FinOps depends on one provider
choices.why: The lesson was written to survive exactly this; it names mechanisms generically for that reason.

prompt: Coreto's cloud bill is R$ 212,000 a month and it sells 410,000 tickets a month. What is the cloud cost per ticket sold, in reais, to three decimal places?
hint: The bill divided by the tickets.

prompt: Otávio sees next year's cloud bill rising 11.3% and asks why engineering is spending more. What does the unit cost let Davi answer?

choices.text: That a rise of 11.3% is normal for any cloud bill
choices.why: There is no normal rise; whether it is good depends on what was sold, which is the point of the unit.

choices.text: That the provider will lower its prices next year
choices.why: Nothing in the plan rests on the provider's prices; it rests on tickets.

choices.text: That engineering will cut the bill back to R$ 212,000
choices.why: The plan expects R$ 236,000, and serving 520,000 tickets on the old bill was never proposed.

choices.text: Each ticket gets 12.2% cheaper to serve
choices.why: Right: R$ 0.517 to R$ 0.454 per ticket. The same plan, read per unit of business.

prompt: Which of these pass the lesson's tests for a unit cost at Coreto? Choose all that apply.
hint: Earned from, stable, and movable by the teams.

choices.text: Cloud cost per server
choices.why: A server is an input; the cost per server says nothing about whether the spending was worth it.

choices.text: Cloud cost per ticket sold
choices.why: Yes: Coreto earns a fee per ticket, so it reads against revenue.

choices.text: Catalogue's cost per search, rolled up to the company's
choices.why: Yes: a team unit the team can move, as long as it adds up to the company's.

choices.text: Cloud cost per engineer
choices.why: Engineers are an input too, and the business does not sell them.

prompt: Tickets grow 26.8% and the bill 11.3%. A director announces that the teams made the platform 12.2% more efficient. What does the lesson say about that claim?
hint: Some of the bill does not grow with tickets.

choices.text: Fixed costs spread over more tickets explain part of it
choices.why: Right: scale lowers the unit cost with nobody changing anything. Ask which part of the bill moved first.

choices.text: The claim is right: unit cost measures efficiency exactly
choices.why: It is the best single number, and it still mixes scale with improvement.

choices.text: The claim is wrong, because the bill went up
choices.why: A rising bill with falling unit cost is the healthy case the lesson describes.

choices.text: The 12.2% is the provider's discount
choices.why: The plan does not assume a discount; the figure comes from the bill and the ticket count.

prompt: Catalogue has R$ 41,000 tagged, out of R$ 183,000 tagged in all; R$ 29,000 is untagged. Shared in proportion, how much of the untagged cost does Catalogue receive, in whole reais?
The column of totals with shares adds up to 211,999, and the bill was R$ 212,000. Why?
hint: Look at the ROUND in each cell.

choices.text: Five roundings did not cancel out
choices.why: Right: five roundings, one real short. Say so on the report, or give the real to the largest share.

choices.text: One team's tag is wrong
choices.why: A wrong tag moves money between teams; it does not change the total.

choices.text: The formula leaves out the untagged row
choices.why: $B$8 is in every cell, so the untagged amount is shared out; only the rounding loses a real.

choices.text: The spreadsheet makes floating-point errors with money
choices.why: A floating-point error would be far below a real; this is ROUND to whole numbers, done five times.

prompt: Box Office tags every resource it owns. Under proportional sharing, what happens to it when another team leaves its resources untagged?
hint: Who pays for the untagged pool?

choices.text: Nothing, its line shows only what it tagged
choices.why: Its line also carries a share of the untagged pool, which the other team just made larger.

choices.text: It is credited for tagging well
choices.why: That is what proportional sharing lacks: nobody is rewarded for tagging.

choices.text: It covers part of their cost
choices.why: Right: the untagged pool is shared by tagged cost, so careful teams cover careless ones. Hence the published untagged percentage.

choices.text: The untagged cost is charged to Platform instead
choices.why: Davi and Rafaela own the untagged percentage as a target; the money is still shared out.

prompt: Match each term to what it means in the lesson.
hint: One of them moves money; one only shows it.

pairs.right: Each team is shown its share of the bill
The cost is charged to the team's own budget
A label on a resource naming its owner
How far to trust the rest of the report

prompt: Put the usual cloud savings in the order the lesson works through them.
hint: Do not sign a contract for waste.
trap: Committing first locks in a year of paying for machines that should have been switched off.

prompt: Idle staging cost Coreto R$ 9,800 a month. How much is that a year, in reais?
Which of Coreto's measures keeps the staging saving from decaying in the way the lesson describes?
hint: A saving that depends on people remembering.

choices.text: An email reminding teams to switch staging off
choices.why: A reminder still depends on people remembering, which is what decays.

choices.text: A one-year commitment on staging capacity
choices.why: That would lock in the very machines the schedule turns off.

choices.text: Staging is off by default
choices.why: Right: leaving it on takes an action instead of forgetting one. That is the operate phase.

choices.text: Moving staging to the cheapest machine class available
choices.why: That is rightsizing; it lowers the price of the waste without stopping it.

prompt: A company sells accounting software as a monthly subscription. Which unit cost fits this lesson's tests best?

choices.text: Cloud cost per server in production
choices.why: An input, as at Coreto; it says nothing about whether the spending was worth it.

choices.text: Cloud cost per line of code shipped
choices.why: The business does not sell lines of code, and the teams would move it in the wrong direction.

choices.text: Cloud cost per paying subscriber in a month
choices.why: Right: the subscription is what it earns from, as the ticket is at Coreto, and it reads against revenue.

choices.text: The total bill, compared with last year's
choices.why: That is the bill alone, which cannot say whether the company got better or merely bigger.

prompt: Staging switched off by default and a monthly review of the bill belong to the FinOps phase called ___.
Mateus wants Coreto to commit to three years of capacity at today's size, for the best rate. What does the lesson tell him to do first?

choices.text: Negotiate a larger discount on the three years
choices.why: A better rate on waste is still waste; the order of the list comes before the price.

choices.text: Move to a different provider with lower prices
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson calls for a move; the waste would travel with Coreto.

choices.text: Rewrite the services that cost most before committing
choices.why: Architecture comes last, and only with the engineering hours priced.

choices.text: Remove the waste first, then commit to what is left
choices.why: Right: committing first signs a contract for the idle staging and the oversized machines.

prompt: Helena suggests chargeback, so that teams feel the cost. Coreto's budget is four company-wide lines. What does the lesson say?
hint: Whose budget would the money move out of?

choices.text: It is the right next step after showback
choices.why: It needs team budgets first, and an allocation everyone accepts; Coreto has neither.

choices.text: It would move money between team budgets that do not exist
choices.why: Right: teams have no budgets of their own, and showback gets most of the effect without one.

choices.text: It works, provided the tags are accurate
choices.why: Accurate tags help, and the missing team budgets are still the obstacle.

choices.text: It should replace showback to save the work of reporting
choices.why: Chargeback needs more reporting rather than less, since every share is now somebody's money.
